tldr: This research trains a visual humanoid loco-manipulation policy entirely on synthetic data in simulation and successfully deploys it zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 robot. The authors show that the performance ceiling caused by behavior cloning (BC) on scripted behaviors can be broken by reinforcement learning with sparse rewards (Flow-GRPO).
hero_caption: Overview of FetchMan and real-world experiments. After cloning behaviors (BC) from a scripted expert across over 150,000 diverse simulated scenes, the policy is refined via Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning. As a result, a real Unitree G1 robot successfully walks up to and grasps target objects across unseen rooms.
overview:
Enabling humanoid robots to walk, approach, and grasp objects in unseen environments—known as visual loco-manipulation—has long been a major goal in robotics. However, real-world data collection carries high risks of falling and high costs, making simulation-based reinforcement learning and imitation learning necessary. A central problem here is that behavior cloning (BC) directly on trajectories automatically generated (scripted) in a simulator hits a performance ceiling, no matter how much data is added. While the scripted expert relies on internal, privileged phase variables such as moving, approaching, and grasping, these boundaries are invisible to the learned policy, which only observes camera images and joint angles. This creates a structural limitation (imitation gap).

To break through this barrier, the authors built "FetchMan," a two-stage training pipeline leveraging a large-scale procedurally generated environment (MolmoSpaces). In the first stage, a Flow-Matching policy is pretrained on scripted demonstrations across 150,000 scenes. In the second stage, taking advantage of a unique simulator capability—parallel group rollouts from identical states—the policy is refined (fine-tuned) using Flow-GRPO with only a simple sparse task success/failure reward. This allows the policy to smoothly resolve the discontinuities of explicit phase transitions on its own.

In simulated benchmark evaluations, this approach boosted the success rate from 67% with BC alone to 83%. Furthermore, in zero-shot transfer experiments to a real Unitree G1 robot, it achieved a 73.3% success rate in unseen office environments. It demonstrates a powerful recipe for integrating humanoid locomotion and manipulation without using any real-world data or per-scene tuning.
contributions: Established a visual humanoid loco-manipulation method that uses over 150,000 diverse simulation scenes to transfer zero-shot to unseen environments without any real-world data.

Identified the mechanism behind performance saturation when cloning a privileged scripted expert, and showed that Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning can break through this ceiling with only a sparse reward.
Constructed and released "FetchMan-Bench," a reproducible evaluation benchmark for humanoid loco-manipulation.
Trained a multi-object generalization model conditioned on text instructions, paving the way toward generalist loco-manipulation policies at this data scale.

sections.heading: Why can't humanoid loco-manipulation be solved by imitation alone?
sections.summary: While simulation has become the standard for humanoid locomotion, adding contact-rich object manipulation dramatically increases the challenge. Furthermore, simply cloning scripted trajectories in simulation hits a performance ceiling due to an imitation gap caused by privileged phase variables. This paper proposes a recipe combining hierarchical control and Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning to break through this ceiling.
sections.details:
For humanoid locomotion, combining simulation with reinforcement learning (RL) has made it possible to build practical policies. However, when object manipulation is added to form loco-manipulation, the problem becomes far more difficult. Modeling contact-rich interactions with the environment is challenging, and the engineering burden of providing diverse environmental assets necessary for visual generalization is immense.

Collecting data on real hardware is also difficult. Unlike fixed arms, humanoids must recover from falls and maintain whole-body balance, drastically increasing the cost and risk per trajectory. One might consider using behavior cloning (BC) on massive datasets collected with scripted controllers (automatically generated trajectories) in simulation, but two major obstacles emerge:

- Imperfection of expert trajectories and the "imitation gap": The scripted expert generating the data relies on internal, discrete phase variables such as "move," "approach," "lower," and "grasp." However, the learned policy, which only observes camera images and proprioception, cannot see these internal phases. As a result, sharp motion discontinuities appear near phase transitions from moving to grasping, making imitation remarkably difficult.
- Covariate shift and objective misalignment: Even with perfect expert data, the objective of imitation learning is to reproduce the expert's actions rather than achieving task success itself. Small errors accumulate, leading the robot into out-of-distribution states.

In this work, the authors compress the control space by freezing a low-level whole-body controller, and combine large-scale simulation BC with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—leveraging identical-state rollouts unique to simulators. This forms "FetchMan," an end-to-end sim-to-real approach that breaks through the imitation ceiling.

sections.heading: Synthetic data generation, humanoid control, and RL for flow policies
sections.summary: Robot learning using large-scale synthetic data, humanoid whole-body teleoperation, and sim-to-real pretraining are actively studied. Recently, reinforcement learning for Flow-Matching policies (such as Flow-GRPO) has emerged. This work integrates these threads and scales them to whole-body reach-and-pick tasks in unseen scenes.
sections.details:
To understand where this work stands, we can look at three related research lines:

- Synthetic Demonstration Generation: To address data scarcity in robotics, synthetic data has been applied to driving and navigation. Recently, systems like MolmoBot have achieved zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in tabletop manipulation. While Behavior1K and RoboCasa365 handle loco-manipulation, their environmental diversity is fixed. This work maintains high physical fidelity while significantly scaling scene and object diversity tailored to humanoids.
- Learning Humanoid Locomotion and Manipulation: Approaches using human motion retargeting and teleoperation (HumanPlus, OmniH2O) as well as VLA models combining real demonstrations and web videos (GR00T-N1, Humanoid-VLA, $\psi_0$) exist, but the cost of collecting real data remains a bottleneck. On the other hand, works like VIRAL and DoorMan achieve zero-shot transfer purely from simulation, but they either focus on limited evaluation environments or require complex, hand-engineered reward functions.
- Post-Training Flow-Based Policies: Highly expressive flow-based (Flow-Matching) and diffusion action heads have been difficult to fine-tune with RL because their action likelihoods are hard to compute analytically. Recently proposed methods such as Flow-GRPO turn the process stochastic by injecting small Gaussian noise into the sampler, making step-by-step likelihood ratios tractable. This work applies Flow-GRPO to humanoid loco-manipulation, bridging the imitation gap using only sparse rewards in simulation.

sections.heading: Robot I/O and hierarchical control architecture
sections.summary: Targeting the Unitree G1 humanoid, the policy takes head fisheye camera, wrist camera, and proprioceptive inputs to output 15-dimensional whole-body commands at 10 Hz. Adopting a pretrained locomotion-balance controller (SONIC) as the low-level controller abstracts away 29-DoF joint torques, making large-scale learning practical.
sections.details:
The hardware platform used for experiments and training is the Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with Dex1-1 grippers. The control system accepts 15-dimensional whole-body commands operating at 10 Hz. This input interface is shared between the scripted controller used for data generation and the learned policy during inference.

The observation space $o_t$ consists of:
- Visual information: Head fisheye camera image $I^{\text{head}}_t$ and right wrist camera image $I^{\text{wrist}}_t$ (both $224 \times 384 \times 3$ RGB images).
- Proprioception $o^{\text{prop}}_t$: Base height $h_t$, base roll $r_t$ and pitch $p_t$, upper-body joint positions $q^{\text{upper}}_t$ (3 waist axes, 7 right arm axes), and right gripper opening $g_t$.

The action space $a_t$ has 15 dimensions:
- Base velocity command $v_t = (v_x, v_y, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (forward, lateral, and yaw angular velocities)
- Target base height $\bar{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}$
- Target upper-body joint positions $\bar{q}^{\text{waist}}_t \in \mathbb{R}^3$, $\bar{q}^{\text{arm}}_t \in \mathbb{R}^7$
- Target right gripper opening $\bar{g}_t \in \mathbb{R}$

Hierarchical Control Structure:
Base velocity and height commands $(v_t, \bar{h}_t)$ are sent to "SONIC," a pretrained low-level controller running at 50 Hz. SONIC is a decoupled controller that switches between standing balance and walking, ultimately translating commands into 200 Hz joint torques. Meanwhile, upper-body and gripper targets are tracked by joint-level PD controllers. This hierarchy dramatically reduces the control space the policy must handle from 29 joint torques to 15 meaningful high-level commands. Furthermore, because identical control stacks run in both simulation and the real world, the low-level controller's response characteristics remain fixed, reducing sim-to-real transfer gaps.

captions.F2: Examples of simulated observation images received by the policy. Left shows the right wrist camera, and right shows the head fisheye camera, illustrating wide domain randomization across textures, lighting, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics.

sections.heading: Pipeline for generating synthetic demos across over 150,000 rooms
sections.summary: Building on MolmoSpaces, the pipeline samples diverse floor plans, objects, and initial poses, which are solved by a scripted controller. Robust training datasets are created through 3D whole-body collision checking for spawning, mixing long-range navigation with close-up picking, and thorough domain randomization.
sections.details:
To automatically generate demonstration trajectories as supervision, a data generation pipeline was built on top of "MolmoSpaces," a procedural indoor environment generator.

- 4.1 Task Sampling: Each episode samples a tuple consisting of a scene $s$, a target object $m$, and the robot's initial pose $x_0$. Scenes are selected from vast indoor environments like ProcTHOR and Holodeck to construct a 2D traversability grid $\mathcal{O}_s$. The robot's initial position is determined within an annulus at a certain distance from the object. Rather than using simple 2D footprint checks, full-body 3D collision checking is performed in the simulator. This allows spawning close to surfaces—even when hands overhang a table—covering diverse real-world approach poses.
- 4.2 Scripted Controller (Expert): The expert policy $\pi_{\text{ctrl}}$ operates with direct access to privileged information, such as the true object pose and occupancy grid. When far from the target, it plans paths using A* search to navigate. Once within grasping range, it transitions through discrete phases: reach $\rightarrow$ lower $\rightarrow$ grasp $\rightarrow$ lift. Using the inverse kinematics (IK) library "Mink," waist height is treated as a free optimization variable, allowing the robot to crouch and dexterously grasp objects at lower heights.
- 4.3 Episode Mixing Ratio: 80% of generated data consists of long-range navigation and grasping ("Fetch"), while the remaining 20% starts directly in front of the target object ("Pick-only"). Mixing pick-only episodes randomizes the initial arm joint angles and gripper openings, giving the policy the generalization capability to handle arm offsets when navigation finishes.
- 4.4 Domain Randomization: To bridge the visual and physical sim-to-real gap, wall and floor textures, light positions, colors, shadows, head and wrist camera field-of-view, distortion, mounting poses, support surface heights, and Gaussian noise injected into control commands are all independently randomized in every episode.

captions.F3: The synthetic data generation pipeline. Demonstrations are sampled across over 150,000 houses and 50,000 objects with domain randomization, where a scripted whole-body controller generates continuous trajectories from navigation through grasping.

sections.heading: Two-stage learning: Grounding with imitation, refining with Flow-GRPO
sections.summary: The architecture adopts DINOv3 as the visual encoder and a Flow-Matching DiT as the action head. Stage 1 performs behavior cloning on synthetic demos, while Stage 2 uses Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning with only sparse success/failure rewards, smoothly overcoming the discontinuous phase boundaries of the scripted expert.
sections.details:
The unprivileged visual policy $\pi_\theta(a \mid o)$ is trained in two stages: pretraining (BC) and reinforcement learning (RL).

- 5.1 Model Architecture: Image inputs are transformed into patch tokens using a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16. The proprioceptive vector is mapped to a single state token via an MLP and concatenated with image tokens. The action head employs a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) Flow-Matching model, predicting an action chunk $a_{t:t+H}$ up to $H=16$ steps ahead via cross-attention over observation tokens. For multi-object models, the vision backbone is replaced with "dino.txt" (aligned text and vision), fusing text tokens of object names into the visual features.
- 5.2 Imitation Pretraining (BC): Behavior cloning is performed on the scripted expert trajectories. Following $\pi_0$, base translational/yaw velocities and gripper opening are predicted as absolute values, while 11 dimensions including base height and arm/waist joint angles are normalized and predicted as delta offsets from current values. At inference time, only the first 8 steps of the 16 predicted steps are executed before re-inferring on the next observation.
- 5.3 Flow-GRPO Refinement: Because the expert relies on privileged discrete phase variables, simple trajectory relabeling like DAgger does not work. Instead, the authors use "Flow-GRPO" to directly optimize the Flow-Matching policy. By injecting small Gaussian noise into Euler integration during inference, the process is formulated as a stochastic differential equation (SDE), making step-by-step log-likelihoods analytically computable. During training, $M=8$ parallel rollouts are generated from a single initial state varying only noise, and the policy is updated using the group's relative reward difference $A_i = (R_i - \mu)/\sigma$ as the advantage without requiring a value network. The reward $R_i$ is completely sparse: 1 if the object is lifted, and 0 otherwise. This allows the policy to self-learn smooth transitions from navigation to manipulation without manual reward shaping.

captions.F4: FetchMan's policy architecture. Features from head and wrist camera images are extracted with frozen DINOv3 and fed into a Flow-Matching DiT alongside proprioceptive tokens. The predicted 15-dimensional action chunk is then sent to low-level PD controllers and the locomotion controller (SONIC).

sections.heading: 73.3% real-world zero-shot success and data scaling limits
sections.summary: Scaling synthetic demonstrations from 50k to 150k plateaued BC success at 67%, but Flow-GRPO RL pushed it up to 83%. Zero-shot deployment on a real Unitree G1 recorded a 73.3% success rate, revealing that DINOv3 and delta action representations are critical for transfer.
sections.details:
Experiments were evaluated using 150k bowl-grasping demonstrations (approximately 650 hours) generated in about 40 hours on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU.

- 6.1 & 6.2 Evaluation Setup and FetchMan-Bench: The authors evaluate on "FetchMan-Bench," a simulation benchmark they developed. Two metrics are used: "Manipulation SR" (grasping directly in front of the object) and "Loco-manipulation SR" (walking from a distance to grasp the object).
- 6.3 Plateau in Data Scaling (RQ1): Increasing demonstrations from 5k to 50k improved the loco-manipulation success rate from 40% to 67%, but expanding further to 150k remained completely saturated at 67%. This proves that the imitation gap caused by invisible expert phase variables cannot be closed by data scaling alone.
- 6.4 Breaking the Ceiling with RL (RQ2): Applying Flow-GRPO to the saturated 150k checkpoint significantly increased the simulation success rate from 67% to 83%. In contrast, applying RL directly to an undertrained 5k-demo model (40% success) only reached about 42% and oscillated. Group relative advantage only works effectively when built on a solid imitation baseline. In real-world evaluations, RL boosted the loco-manipulation success rate from 56.7% to 73.3%.
- 6.5 Ablations for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer (RQ3): Investigating the drivers of the 73.3% real-world success rate revealed that replacing the DINOv3 backbone with SigLIP dropped real success to 0% (DINOv3's strong geometric representation is essential). Switching action representation from delta to absolute values also resulted in 0% real-world success, showing both design choices are vital for sim-to-real transfer.
- 6.6 Multi-Object Generalization (RQ4): Training a text-conditioned model on 350k demonstrations improved simulation success from 40% (BC) to 62% after RL. The real G1 also succeeded in zero-shot grasping across multiple categories, including bread, bottles, plush toys, and towels.

captions.F6: Zero-shot deployment on the real Unitree G1 (left) and behavioral differences after RL refinement (right). The BC-only policy tends to overextend its arms from too far away and fail, whereas Flow-GRPO refinement trains the robot to step closer, lower its waist, and grasp securely.
captions.F7: Learning curves demonstrating data scaling saturation and RL breakthrough. In the left plot, BC plateaus at 67% success beyond 50k demos, but subsequent GRPO (red line) shoots up to 83%. The right plot shows progress on the multi-object model.
captions.F8: Head camera views of multi-object grasping on the real robot using the text-conditioned policy. The robot approaches and grasps diverse items—such as a pot, bread, bottle, plush elephant, book, towel, and headphones—based on specified names.

sections.heading: Current limitations and future outlook
sections.summary: This method has three main limitations: a stateless design without observation history, limited adaptation due to a frozen low-level locomotion controller, and tasks restricted to simple picking. Scaling compute and model capacity will be important future steps.
sections.details:
The paper candidly discusses the following limitations:

- Stateless Architecture Without History: The policy takes only a single frame of images and proprioception as input, without past observation history. This makes inferring the scripted expert's internal phase inherently difficult. While frame stacking could help, it was omitted here because it significantly increases visual token counts and computational cost.
- Frozen Low-Level Locomotion Controller: Because the underlying SONIC controller is frozen, the robot cannot adapt by bracing itself when carrying heavy items or widening its stance to reach further. Learning whole-body torque control end-to-end could solve this, but learning balance from scratch causes training costs to explode.
- Task Diversity: The scope was limited to a single task: walking to and picking up an object ("Fetch"). Extending this framework to more complex, long-horizon tasks like opening doors or drawers remains future work.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: By combining synthetic simulation data with Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning, FetchMan demonstrates an end-to-end framework where a real humanoid walks and grasps in unseen environments. Uncovering the hidden limits of synthetic imitation and showing the effectiveness of RL refinement represents a major step forward.
sections.details:
This work presented "FetchMan," a visual humanoid loco-manipulation system trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 robot.

Demonstrations were generated using a scripted controller across hundreds of thousands of procedural scenes. A Flow-Matching policy was pretrained with behavior cloning and then refined via Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning with sparse rewards. Experiments revealed that imitation learning alone plateaus due to the hidden phase structure of scripted experts, and that group-relative RL breaks this ceiling, achieving a high success rate of 73.3% on real hardware.

Furthermore, the approach successfully extended to text-conditioned multi-object grasping, providing highly practical and valuable guidelines toward generalist humanoid robots powered by large-scale simulation.

takeaways: No matter how many synthetic scripted demonstrations are added, BC performance hits a ceiling due to invisible privileged phase variables (imitation gap); RL refinement is essential.
Because simulators can run parallel rollouts from identical states at zero real-world cost, value-network-free GRPO (Flow-GRPO) works remarkably well and reliably.
Adopting a vision backbone with rich geometric representations (DINOv3) and formulating the action space as delta offsets are decisive factors for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

Freezing a low-level balance controller to abstract actions into high-level commands (velocities and joint targets) compresses 29-DoF whole-body control into 15 dimensions, enabling efficient large-scale RL.
limitations: The single-frame stateless observation structure requires the policy to infer motion context and phase from just one snapshot.
Because the low-level locomotion controller (SONIC) is frozen, the robot cannot perform flexible whole-body coordination, such as crouching low or widening its stance for heavy objects.
Evaluations are limited to object pick-up ("Fetch"), leaving generalization to long-horizon tasks with contact constraints (e.g., opening drawers or doors) unverified.
